title: After Wang Fuk Court
deck: Finding a place to live after the Wang Fuk Court fire
subtitle: What it takes to settle again after Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in over 70 years.
excerpt: What it takes to settle again after Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in over 70 years. For this independent follow-up, I contacted the Hong Kong Red Cross about the recovery and examined published personal accounts alongside government records.

content.alt: People watching the burning towers of Wang Fuk Court at night in Tai Po, Hong Kong
content.caption: People watch the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, Hong Kong, on November 26, 2025.

content.text: Ms. Chu spent a week in hospital and needed a place to live, but due to mobility issues could not move into a transitional apartment on the third floor. Her husband eventually found a ground-floor flat in Yuen Long, and the couple moved in mid-December.
Ms. Chu's story is told in a report published by the Hong Kong Red Cross, which identifies her by a pseudonym. It describes a small part of the work that followed her rescue.

168 people died and almost 2,000 households were displaced by the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po on November 26, 2025, according to Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong. People needed a place to live while coping with the loss of their belongings and, sometimes, relatives.

These stories drew my attention to the practical aspects of providing assistance. The housing has to suit the residents, and the application process needs a way of checking eligibility. Applicants sometimes need additional time to talk at the registration desk.

By September the government buyout program had already involved the majority of the property owners. According to the Housing Bureau's update of September 3, 1,971 owners across the estate's eight blocks had confirmed their intention to sell their property titles, and 1,595 households had signed sale-and-purchase agreements as of September 2. These numbers show the progress of flat purchases; however, they do not show how many families managed to find permanent replacement homes.

Understanding the recovery process requires taking into account not only the signing of the buyout agreement but also the availability of suitable accommodation, the journeys it requires and whether daily tasks are manageable there. All these should be considered alongside progress on the buyout.

According to Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong, its response has included providing household items — beds, wardrobes, tables, chairs, kettles, and rice cookers — to the affected families. The organization also describes work towards a three-year housing assistance program, with input from social workers, housing operators and residents. Although these items are basic household goods, acquiring them requires money, delivery arrangements and space in the new accommodation. The listed items show what tasks are associated with the creation of a new home.

content.text: Issues with the provision of emergency assistance arose several days after the fire. In a letter dated 1 December 2025, the Hong Kong Social Workers General Union noted difficulties distinguishing owners from tenants that delayed financial assistance for some households. The union called on aid organizations to give priority to actual residence when deciding eligibility for assistance.

Moreover, the Hong Kong Social Workers General Union raised the possibility that identity cards and tenancy agreements had been destroyed and suggested using social worker referrals or sworn declarations as alternative documentation. Though this letter describes issues encountered during aid delivery, it does not give the number of affected families or establish how particular cases were resolved.

It is important to verify applications in order to protect limited funds, but the requested documentation may be among the things lost in the fire. The union proposed alternative ways to verify applications so that missing documentation would not prevent people from receiving aid.

In addition, a volunteer's account, published on Tzu Chi's Jing Si website on December 12, 2025, reveals another obstacle in providing aid. On the first Saturday after the fire, a distraught resident directed an outburst at volunteers. Then a team leader sat with the resident on a bench by a park, giving her time to regain her composure before helping her register.

Giving people time is an important, but often underrated, element of relief work. In this story, the volunteer stayed with the distraught resident until she was calmer before continuing the registration process.

Another challenge in providing relief assistance is mentioned by Charmaine, a psychological-support volunteer with the Red Cross, in an account published by the organization. She described the additional strain on bereaved family members when sharing their experiences left friends and relatives so distressed that the bereaved themselves had to provide comfort.

These stories raise questions about the practices of relief organizations. A family may need a quick decision while someone in it needs more time to talk about what happened. Staff on the ground should be prepared for both.

Nevertheless, the limitations of these records should be considered. Charities select stories to show their work, and the limited number of published accounts cannot represent every family's experience. These stories describe particular problems that arose after the fire and cannot establish whether the same problems remain unresolved today.

However, despite these limitations, the stories raise questions relevant to the current recovery: can residents manage in the accommodation offered? Is it possible to verify applications when the usual documents are missing? Is there someone who can listen without placing additional demands on the person seeking help? Answers to these questions can provide more insight into how aid is provided.
For Ms. Chu, suitable accommodation meant a ground-floor flat. Finding it took another search.

reportingNote: Months after the fire at Wang Fuk Court, I contacted the Hong Kong Red Cross to find out how people who had lost relatives or been forced from their homes were doing: whether they could access financial assistance, find suitable accommodation and begin to return to everyday life. This article draws on published personal accounts made available by the Red Cross and other organisations, alongside government records.
